intro: Scarlatti’s Sonata in E major, K. 380, marked Andante commodo, is in triple time, with trills on its repeated notes and sudden runs up the keyboard. Marcelle Meyer plays it on the piano.

sections.label: A · Repeated notes and trills
sections.mNote: Three-beat phrases modulate from E major to B major.

sections.label: A · First half repeated, E major
B · New phrase over B
sections.mNote: The second half begins in the dominant key.

sections.label: B · Second half, returning to E
sections.mNote: The second half modulates back to E major.

cues.title: Opening phrase with trills
cues.text: The opening phrase steps down, followed by three repeated notes, each with a trill. The three-beat metre stays clear. The hands take turns with the short descending figure before the runs begin.
cues.evidence: Scarlatti, Sonata K. 380, piano edition reproduced as IMSLP 691879, bars 1–12. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Arrival in Lisbon, 1719
cues.text: Scarlatti arrived in Lisbon on 29 November 1719. At the palace he sang while Queen Maria Anna accompanied him. Among his new pupils was her daughter Maria Bárbara, whose service later took him to Spain.
cues.evidence: Cristina Fernandes, Scarlatti, Giuseppe Domenico, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, vol. 91 (2018), citing the papal nuncio’s account of Scarlatti’s arrival. https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giuseppe-domenico-scarlatti_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/

cues.title: Repeat of the opening, bar 40
cues.text: The first half has reached B major, a fifth above the home key. At the repeat in bar 40, E major returns with the descending phrase and its three trills from bars 1–4. For the first few bars the left hand rests and the right hand plays alone.
cues.evidence: Piano edition, first repeat at bar 40, returning to bars 1–4. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Address to the reader, 1738
cues.text: In the address to the reader of his Essercizi, published in 1738, Scarlatti offered “art’s ingenious play” to develop fluency at the harpsichord. The invitation was addressed to amateurs and professionals alike.
cues.evidence: Our translation of “lo scherzo ingegnoso dell’arte” from Scarlatti’s address to the reader, Essercizi per gravicembalo (London, 1738), quoted by Cristina Fernandes: https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giuseppe-domenico-scarlatti_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/.

cues.title: Opening of the second half
cues.text: The second half begins in B major, the key in which the first half ended. The left hand plays repeated bass notes and the right hand has a new phrase. The metre is still triple, and the music now moves towards E major.
cues.evidence: Piano edition, bars 41–44 and the E-major ending. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repeat of the second half
cues.text: After the cadence in E major, the piano returns to the start of the second half, and the repeated notes and quick ornaments are played again. The sonata ends at bar 78 with a falling run, a trill and a final E in the bass.
cues.evidence: Piano edition, second-half repeat and final bars, ending at bar 78. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From B major back to E major
transitions.to: A · First half repeated, E major
transitions.how: A descending run and a trill close the first half in B major. At the repeat the right hand plays the opening E major phrase again, which begins with three repeated trills. The left hand rests for the first four bars.
transitions.evidence: Piano edition, bars 39–40 followed by bars 1–4. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf

transitions.title: Second half begins in B major
transitions.from: A · First half repeated, E major
transitions.how: The first half closes in B major, and the new phrase that opens the second half is also in B major. The left hand moves from the held cadential bass into repeated notes. Above it, the right hand plays short repeated notes and a rising run.

transitions.title: E major close and return to B
transitions.to: B · Second half, returning to E
transitions.how: The final descending run ends on E, with the same note low in the bass. When the repeat is taken, the music returns to the B major opening of the second half. After the held ending, the left hand resumes its regular three-beat accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Piano edition, bars 77–78 and return to bar 41. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Both recording sources identify Meyer; the chronology identifies the Scarlatti piano session. No historical keyboard type is inferred from the composition’s age.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Solo piano performance of the keyboard sonata
fields.note: A single complete sonata is hosted, not a movement from a multi-movement set. The date 1754 is retained as a Venice-manuscript copy date, not a proven composition date. Meyer’s edition and editorial interventions are unknown. The Longo reference score’s fingering, dynamics and other editorial directions are not attributed to Scarlatti or to Meyer. The two repeated halves are mapped provisionally from the score and audio report, not a note-by-note alignment.

composer.epithet: Composer and royal teacher, known for his keyboard sonatas.
facts: Alessandro Scarlatti’s sixth child; born in 1685, the year of Bach and Handel
Maria Bárbara of Portugal, later Queen of Spain; he served her until his death
Naples and Rome; Lisbon from 1719; Spain from 1729
555 in Ralph Kirkpatrick’s catalogue; most survive in manuscript copies
composer.background:
On 30 May 1705 Alessandro Scarlatti wrote to Ferdinando de’ Medici about his nineteen-year-old son Domenico: “This son is an eagle whose wings have grown; he must not idle in the nest, and I must not prevent his flight.” Domenico already held a post as organist at the royal chapel in Naples and had written operas. His father sent him north towards Venice, by way of Florence, with this recommendation. Domenico later settled much farther from home, as teacher to a Portuguese princess whose marriage took them both to Spain.

Domenico was born in Naples on 26 October 1685, the same year as J. S. Bach and Handel, the sixth of Alessandro’s ten children. His family included singers as well as composers, and several of them worked in opera. He became a salaried royal organist at fifteen. In Rome he served Maria Casimira, the widowed Queen of Poland, who maintained a theatre in her Palazzo Zuccari. Scarlatti supplied her with seven operas between 1710 and 1714, working with the poet Carlo Sigismondo Capece and the stage designer Filippo Juvarra.
